newsitem.title: USA: U.S. business group blasts trade sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. business group blasts trade sanctions.

text.p: An influential U.S business group Wednesday sharply criticised the use of trade sanctions to achieve foreign policy objectives and said their cost to the U.S. economy should be examined.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce singled out the so-called Helms-Burton law aimed at foreign investment in Cuba and the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act, which targets large investments in those countries, as examples of bad laws with good intentions. Both laws were enacted this year.

In a statement issued after a meeting of the chamber's board of directors, the group said those laws and other unilateral sanctions promised "further isolation of U.S. foreign policy, reinforced rather than weakened hostile regimes and diminution of economic opportunity for U.S. firms and their workers."
The statement, issued after an annual meeting of the board of directors, calls on the government to conduct annual surveys on the cost of each sanction to the U.S. economy.
Any new legislation proposing sanctions should also be subjected to a cost-benefit analysis, the group said.
The group also urged the government to clarify commercial policies toward Russia and work to improve trade opportunities for U.S. companies.

It also urged quick passage of so-called fast track trade negotiating authority, which would allow the Clinton administration to negotiate trade deals without fear they later will be changed by Congress.

The legislation, which was put on hold during the presidential election campaign, is needed for U.S. negotitions with Chile to bring it into the North American Free Trade Agreement and to negotiate a hemispheric free-trade accord.

The group also urged U.S. lawmakers to grant permanent preferential trade privileges to China. The privileges allow Chinese goods to enter the country at the same low tariffs as goods from most other countries.
Only a handful of countries do not enjoy the privileges, and the business group said ending the annual ritual of renewing China's trade status was important for U.S. long-term interests.
China's trade privileges have often been challenged because of human rights, nuclear proliferation and other issues.
